title: Manitou Springs Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Manitou Springs wells have a 63 ft median depth, 8 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $9,200-$16,700.
h1: Manitou Springs Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Manitou Springs means looking past the view and checking the well record. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,598 permitted wells, although only 860 are recorded as constructed. Depth, production, water level, and permit purpose vary considerably because the area includes fractured bedrock, alluvial ground, homes, and monitoring sites.

The nearby record includes Cascade-Chipita Park, Green Mountain Falls, Colorado Springs, Stratmoor, and other parts of El Paso County. Use the numbers below as a screening tool, not as a guarantee for one parcel. A neighboring well can help, but a driller still needs to evaluate the exact lot.

sections.heading: Manitou Springs well depths vary sharply by ground
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Manitou Springs is 63 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 300 feet, which is a wide bidding range for a buyer. Fifty-seven percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 23% fall between 300 and 600 feet. Four percent are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest record reaches 1,025 feet.

That spread reflects the local mix of sedimentary and alluvial ground along with the dominant unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. A 63-foot median does not mean every homesite will be shallow. For a drilling estimate, ask for nearby completed logs, casing and grout assumptions, and the price if the hole must continue beyond the expected target.

sections.heading: Most Manitou Springs wells make usable household flow
sections.html:
Among the 296 records reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 10.0 gpm, and 69% falls between 5 and 15 gpm. Only 2% report less than 1 gpm, while 21% report 1 to 5 gpm and 8% report more than 15 gpm.

That is a generally workable production profile for domestic use, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed daily supply. A low-producing well may still work with a storage tank, while a good pump test does not resolve water quality. Confirm the permitted use, pump performance, and any test conditions before relying on the result for a household.

sections.heading: Water levels near Manitou Springs do not show a simple decline
sections.html:
The median static water level is 90 feet below ground surface, based on 66 records. The middle half is 40 to 170 feet. That range matters when estimating pump setting, trench work, and electrical requirements, but measurements from one property do not establish the level at another.

By measurement decade, the median was 105 feet in the 2000s, 27 feet in the 2010s, and 90 feet in the 2020s. The series moves up and down rather than showing a steady drop. Because the sample is limited and the wells may be in different settings, request the original well construction and water-level records instead of treating the decade figures as a parcel-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long use and changing purposes
sections.html:
Permits in the five-mile area go back to the 1950s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The largest decade was the 1990s with 420 permits, followed by 339 in the 2000s. The records include 50% domestic or household wells and 38% monitoring wells; stock and irrigation each account for 1%.

Most named aquifers are unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, covering 1,478 records. Thirty are listed as alluvial, and 1% identify a Denver Basin aquifer. The most active listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Mountain Well Improvement LLC (Wiley, David D.), and Woods Drilling Inc. (Woods, William L.). Verify the current contractor, license, scope, and permit before signing work.

sections.heading: A Manitou Springs well can cost more than the hole itself
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in this area, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 63-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,200 to $4,700. That is only the hole, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,200 to $16,700 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median site, difficult access, extra casing or grout, or a low-yield design can change the bid. Ask each driller to separate footage, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Check contamination, dry-hole exposure, and the building plan
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention around Manitou Springs. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 121 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 68 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove a particular well is affected, but they are a reason to obtain a current laboratory test and review nearby environmental records.

Low yield and dry-hole risk remain separate from contamination. Fractured rock can produce uneven results over short distances. Before building, confirm the well permit allows the intended household use, locate septic and replacement areas, and make sure access works for a drill rig. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask about augmentation requirements before counting on new indoor or outdoor use.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Manitou Springs lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel and compare completed wells nearby, including depth, yield, static water level, aquifer description, and permit use. Records from Colorado Springs, Cascade-Chipita Park, Green Mountain Falls, and other nearby areas can provide context, but they should not replace logs from the same drainage, road, or geologic feature.

For an existing home, request the well permit, construction report, pump information, treatment history, and recent water test. For vacant land, get a driller’s site review and a written estimate that explains what happens if the first target is dry or produces less than expected. Coordinate the well location with septic setbacks, driveway access, utility trenching, and the planned building footprint before excavation begins.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Manitou Springs?
faq.a: The median reported depth within 5 miles of Manitou Springs is 63 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 300 feet, 57% are under 100 feet, and the deepest record is 1,025 feet. That spread reflects mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground and fractured bedrock, so nearby completed logs matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Manitou Springs?
faq.a: Among 296 records reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gpm, and 69% report 5 to 15 gpm. A yield result is not a guarantee of daily supply, so buyers should review the pump test, storage setup, and permitted household use.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Manitou Springs?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 63-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,200 to $4,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,200 to $16,700. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout, or low yield can change the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Manitou Springs?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Within about 10 miles, records map 121 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 68 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A buyer should obtain a current laboratory test and review local environmental records, especially when a property is near mining or cleanup features.

faq.q: Do Manitou Springs wells have enough water for a home?
faq.a: The reported yield profile is generally favorable for domestic wells: the median is 8.0 gpm, 69% report 5 to 15 gpm, and 2% report under 1 gpm. Still, production varies by fractured-bedrock setting. Confirm the permit, pump performance, storage, and any augmentation requirements before assuming the well supports a home or outdoor uses.
